clinicalPearls: A Joubert-related ciliopathy combining a cerebellar and brainstem malformation with ocular, hepatic and renal disease
Neuroimaging shows the molar tooth sign produced by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and a deepened interpeduncular fossa
Ocular features include severe visual impairment with a Leber-like retinal dystrophy and oculomotor abnormalities
Cystic kidney disease, of nephronophthisis or polycystic type, progresses towards renal failure
Hepatic fibrosis may develop, sometimes with features overlapping the COACH phenotype
Hypotonia, developmental delay and an abnormal neonatal breathing pattern are typical of the Joubert group
Best regarded as part of the Joubert syndrome and related disorders spectrum rather than an isolated entity
reference.pathophysiology: Arima syndrome is one of the Joubert syndrome and related disorders, a group of ciliopathies caused by variants in genes whose products function at the primary cilium and its basal body. Defective ciliary signalling disrupts the mid-hindbrain development that gives rise to the cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and abnormal superior cerebellar peduncles seen radiologically as the molar tooth sign. Because the same specialised cilia are essential in retinal photoreceptors, renal tubular epithelium and the developing biliary plate, the disorder also produces a severe retinal dystrophy, a cystic or nephronophthisis-type kidney disease and hepatic fibrosis. This multi-organ involvement, together with the neonatal breathing abnormality and hypotonia, places Arima syndrome firmly within the molar-tooth ciliopathies alongside classical Joubert and COACH syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: COACH syndrome (vermis hypoplasia, oligophrenia, ataxia, coloboma and hepatic fibrosis)
Leber congenital amaurosis with renal disease
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to identify the molar tooth sign and vermis hypoplasia
Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for retinal dystrophy
Renal ultrasound and renal function testing for nephronophthisis or cystic disease
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for fibrosis
Molecular testing with a Joubert / ciliopathy gene panel
redFlags: An abnormal neonatal breathing pattern with episodic tachypnoea and apnoea
reference.prognosis: The outlook is guarded because of multi-organ involvement; neurodevelopmental impairment is usual, and the long-term course is largely determined by the severity of the renal and hepatic disease.
pitfalls: Overlooking the molar tooth sign and missing the Joubert-related diagnosis
Attributing visual failure to isolated retinal disease and neglecting renal and hepatic surveillance
Failing to monitor liver and kidney function over time
Treating it as a distinct disorder rather than part of the Joubert spectrum
management: Recognise there is no curative therapy, so management is supportive across the affected organ systems
Provide neurodevelopmental support with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy and educational input, while monitoring the abnormal neonatal breathing pattern
Offer low-vision support and ophthalmological management of the Leber-like retinal dystrophy and oculomotor abnormalities
Monitor and manage nephronophthisis or cystic kidney disease, progressing to renal replacement therapy or transplantation as function declines
Undertake hepatic surveillance and manage fibrosis and its portal-hypertension complications
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurology, nephrology, hepatology and ophthalmology through a ciliopathy service
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given the inherited ciliopathy
